title: CPU pipeline stages (classic 5-stage)
summary: The classic 5-stage RISC pipeline: IF (Instruction Fetch), ID (Instruction Decode + Register Read), EX (Execute/ALU), MEM (Memory Access), WB (Write Back). Each stage takes one clock cycle. Hazards: structural (resource conflict), data (RAW/WAR/WAW dependencies), control (branch). Solutions: forwarding/bypassing, stalling, branch prediction, out-of-order execution.

structure.meaning: Fetch instruction from memory (I-cache). Compute next PC (PC+4 or branch target).
Decode instruction. Read source registers from register file. Sign-extend immediate.
ALU operation. Compute branch target. Evaluate branch condition.
Load/store to data cache. (NOP for non-memory instructions.)
Write result to register file. (NOP for stores and branches.)
Read After Write: instruction needs a result that hasn't been written yet. Solved by forwarding or stalling.
Write After Read: less common in in-order pipelines. Solved by register renaming in OoO.
Write After Write: two instructions write the same register. Solved by register renaming in OoO.
Branch outcome unknown until EX stage. Solved by branch prediction and flushing on misprediction.
Two instructions need the same resource (e.g., single-ported memory). Solved by duplicating resources or stalling.

notes: Modern CPUs use deeper pipelines (10-20+ stages) and out-of-order execution.
Out-of-order execution: instructions execute when their operands are ready, not in program order.
Register renaming eliminates WAR and WAW hazards by mapping architectural registers to physical registers.
Reorder buffer (ROB) ensures in-order commit for precise exceptions.
Superscalar: multiple instructions issued per cycle (2-8+).
